title: Water treatment plant: start-up from cold

p: Start the water treatment plant from standstill, from the river to the demineralised water the train is fed with. Its own control desk (
) works it; the main control room only sees its overview.
One pump first: the raw water main fills without a surge; the second follows once the flow is steady.
1–2 mg/L of chlorine keeps algae and slime out of the clarifiers and filters. It must be taken out again before the RO.
The coagulant has to be spread through the water in seconds: an intense mix, then slow flocculation.

text: Set the coagulant dose to the season's jar-test value, 30 mg/L, at the coagulant skid (

p: Ferric chloride neutralises the charge on the clay particles so that they gather into flocs. Too little and the clarifiers carry floc over; too much does no better and makes more sludge. A flood needs more (up to 80 mg/L).
A fraction of a milligram per litre binds the small flocs into large ones that settle fast.

text: ): the plant's full flow, about 1,050 m³/h.

p: The sludge blanket has to form before the clarifiers clear: the filters behind them would block quickly on turbid water.

Start cooling tower makeup pump A (

p: The first train's cooling tower basin takes its makeup from here: without it the basin falls.

text: Start the RO's chemical dosing: sodium bisulphite (

p: Bisulphite takes out the chlorine, which would destroy the polyamide membranes; antiscalant and acid keep salts from scaling them as the concentrate thickens.
Above 300 mV the RO trips: free chlorine reaches the membranes.
It strips the carbon dioxide the RO lets through, which would otherwise load the mixed beds.

text: ): a 30-minute low-pressure flush, then the high-pressure pump (
) ramps up with the permeate to drain for the first hour.

p: The flush pushes air and the stagnant water out at 2–4 bar: a membrane must not see a pressure shock. The first permeate is poor until the elements have flushed out ([FT] §5.2).
